content: MUC1, also known as Mucin 1 or polymorphic epithelial mucin (PEM), is a glycoprotein encoded by the MUC1 gene in humans. It is characterized by extensive O-linked glycosylation in its extracellular domain. MUC1 is primarily located on the apical surface of epithelial cells in various organs, including the lungs, stomach, intestines, and eyes. Its primary function is to protect the body from infections by binding pathogens to the oligosaccharides in its extracellular domain, thereby preventing pathogens from reaching the cell surface. Overexpression of MUC1 is frequently associated with cancers such as colon, breast, ovarian, lung, and pancreatic cancers. The antigen was first identified and characterized by Joyce Taylor-Papadimitriou during her research on breast and ovarian tumors. Structure of MUC1 MUC1 belongs to the mucin family and encodes a membrane-bound, glycosylated phosphoprotein. The core protein of MUC1 has a molecular mass of 120-225 kDa, which increases to 250-500 kDa after glycosylation. The protein extends 200-500 nm beyond the cell surface and is anchored to the apical surface of epithelial cells via a transmembrane domain. Adjacent to the transmembrane domain is a SEA domain, which contains a cleavage site for the release of the large extracellular domain. This cleavage is mediated by enzymes known as sheddases. The extracellular domain of MUC1 includes a variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) region, consisting of 20 amino acid repeats. The number of repeats varies between 20 and 120 among individuals. These repeats are rich in serine, threonine, and proline residues, which facilitate heavy O-glycosylation. Multiple alternatively spliced transcript variants of MUC1 have been reported, encoding different isoforms, although the full-length nature of only some variants has been determined. MUC1 undergoes cleavage in the endoplasmic reticulum, resulting in two distinct components: the cytoplasmic tail (which includes the transmembrane domain) and the extracellular domain. These two domains remain tightly associated in a non-covalent manner, resistant to disruption by urea, low pH, high salt concentrations, or boiling. However, treatment with sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) can dissociate the subunits. The cytoplasmic tail of MUC1 is 72 amino acids long and contains several phosphorylation sites. Function of MUC1 MUC1 serves a dual role in cellular protection and signaling. It protects epithelial cells by binding to pathogens, preventing their interaction with the cell surface. Additionally, MUC1 plays a role in cell signaling, particularly in the context of cancer. Overexpression, abnormal intracellular localization, and altered glycosylation of MUC1 are associated with various carcinomas. For example, the CanAg tumor antigen represents a novel glycoform of MUC1. In the cell nucleus, MUC1 regulates transcription factor complexes involved in tumor-induced changes in host immunity. This regulatory function highlights its role in cancer progression. Diagnostic Utility In histopathology, the product of the MUC1 gene is commonly referred to as epithelial membrane antigen (EMA). Immunohistochemical techniques can identify EMA in a wide range of secretory epithelia and their neoplastic counterparts. EMA is also used to identify mesenchymal tumors, such as synovial sarcoma and ovarian granulosa cell tumors. While cytokeratins are more commonly employed for identifying metastatic carcinoma deposits, EMA can help distinguish mesothelioma (where it is restricted to cell membranes and associated microvilli) from adenocarcinoma (where it is diffusely distributed in the cytoplasm). Interactions MUC1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including: CTNND1 (catenin delta-1), ERBB2 (HER2/neu), GRB2 (growth factor receptor-bound protein 2), JUP (junction plakoglobin), and SOS1 (son of sevenless homolog 1). Role in Cancer The extracellular domain of MUC1 is heavily glycosylated, creating a highly hydrophilic region that inhibits the penetration of hydrophobic chemotherapeutic drugs. This glycosylation also binds growth factors, allowing cancer cells to concentrate these factors near their receptors, thereby enhancing receptor activity and promoting cancer cell growth. Furthermore, MUC1 sterically hinders immune cell interactions with cancer cell surface receptors, suppressing anti-tumor immune responses. Preventing Cell Death The cytoplasmic tail of MUC1 interacts with the tumor suppressor protein p53, particularly under conditions of genotoxic stress. This interaction occurs at the p53 response element of the p21 gene promoter, leading to the activation of p21 and subsequent cell cycle arrest. In cancer, the association of MUC1 with p53 inhibits p53-mediated apoptosis while promoting p53-mediated cell cycle arrest. Overexpression of MUC1 in fibroblasts has been shown to increase Akt phosphorylation. Akt phosphorylation leads to the activation of anti-apoptotic pathways, including the dissociation of the Bcl-2-associated death promoter (BAD) from Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL. This process is dependent on upstream activation of PI3K. Additionally, MUC1 overexpression increases the expression of Bcl-xL, preventing the release of cytochrome c from mitochondria and thereby inhibiting apoptosis. The cytoplasmic tail of MUC1 is transported to mitochondria through its interaction with heat shock protein 90 (hsp90). This interaction is induced by phosphorylation of the MUC1 cytoplasmic tail by Src kinase, which is activated by the EGF receptor ligand neuregulin. Once localized to the mitochondria, MUC1 prevents the activation of apoptotic mechanisms. Promoting Tumor Invasion The cytoplasmic tail of MUC1 interacts with beta-catenin, a key component of the Wnt signaling pathway. A conserved SXXXXXSSL motif in MUC1 facilitates this interaction, which is dependent on cell adhesion. MUC1 is phosphorylated at a YEKV motif by kinases such as LYN (mediated by interleukin-7), Src (mediated by EGFR), and PRKCD. This phosphorylation prevents the degradation of beta-catenin by GSK3B, leading to increased stabilization of beta-catenin. Stabilized beta-catenin promotes the expression of mesenchymal markers such as vimentin and CDH2, facilitating epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and enhancing cancer cell motility and invasiveness. This process contributes to metastasis formation. These markers are commonly used in breast cancer diagnostics. CA 27-29 has greater sensitivity and specificity compared to CA 15-3. Elevated levels of CA 27-29 are observed in 30% of patients with early-stage breast cancer and 60-70% of patients with advanced-stage disease. CA 27-29 levels above 100 U/mL and CA 15-3 levels above 25 U/mL are rare in benign conditions and suggest malignancy. Diagnostic Use in Clinical Pathology MUC1 is used as a diagnostic marker for various tumors, including: Adenocarcinomas (breast, colorectal, pancreatic, and others), Carcinoid tumors, Chordomas, Choriocarcinomas, Desmoplastic small round cell tumors (DSRCT), Epithelioid sarcomas, Follicular dendritic cell sarcomas, Lung lesions (e.g., type II pneumocyte hyperplasia), Anaplastic large-cell lymphomas, Epithelioid mesotheliomas, Myelomas and plasmacytomas, Renal cell carcinomas, Synovial sarcomas, and Thymic carcinomas. MUC1 is typically negative in tumors such as adrenal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, germ cell tumors (except choriocarcinoma), leiomyosarcomas, liposarcomas, melanomas, neuroblastomas, and paragangliomas. Therapeutic Target MUC1 is being investigated as a therapeutic target, particularly in the development of cancer vaccines. For example, the MUC1 vaccine ONT-10 has undergone phase 1 clinical trials. These vaccines aim to activate the immune system by training T-cells to recognize and destroy cells expressing tumor-associated MUC1. This approach has potential applications in treating a wide range of cancers, including both solid and non-solid tumors. MUC1 is overexpressed in cancer cells, and its associated glycans are shorter than those found in non-tumor-associated MUC1, making it a promising target for immunotherapy.
